summary: MBW explains why Sony Music and its artists are absent from YouTube's 'Dream Track' AI voice-cloning experiment, which launched November 16 with licensed voices from Universal and Warner artists. Sony took an 'artist-led' approach and its artists were unenthusiastic, and Google's October 30 US Copyright Office filing arguing AI training is fair use reportedly alarmed Sony. The article contrasts Google's position with YouTube's reassurances to the music industry and with UMG's own filing, and wonders if superstars will join later.
one_line: Sony Music stayed out of YouTube's Dream Track AI voice experiment, reportedly because artists were reluctant and Google's USCO fair-use filing alarmed the label.
key_facts: On November 16, 2023 YouTube unveiled 'Dream Track', an experiment letting creators clone the vocals of well-known stars via AI with official consent.
Charlie Puth, John Legend and Demi Lovato are among the voices in Dream Track, alongside artists signed to Warner Music Group and Universal Music Group.
Sony Music Entertainment, the world's second-biggest recording company, has given no endorsement and none of its artists are involved.
MBW understands Sony had been in discussions with YouTube for months about licensing Dream Track.
Sony is taking an 'artist-led' approach to AI experiments; it first offered Dream Track to a number of artists, who showed no enthusiasm.
Bad Bunny, signed to Sony's The Orchard, expressed fury about a popular TikTok track that cloned his vocal stylings via AI.
On October 30, Google filed a submission with the US Copyright Office arguing that AI training on copyrighted material is fair use, which caused alarm at Sony Music HQ.
Google's filing said 'Any prohibition or limitation on the use of copyrighted materials for purposes of Al training would therefore undermine the purpose of copyright'.

In August YouTube and UMG announced an 'AI Music Incubator', and YouTube committed to three principles for its music generative AI tools, then announced a system for removing content that 'mimics an artist's unique singing or rapping voice'.
UMG's own USCO filing said the 'wholesale appropriation' of its catalog to build multibillion commercial AI enterprises 'is anything but fair use'.
YouTube says it paid over USD $6 billion to music rightsholders in the year to end of June 2022, around $2 billion from ads on user-generated content.
The Dream Track artists are not the biggest megastars on UMG's or WMG's rosters; Drake, Taylor Swift, The Beatles, Ed Sheeran and Dua Lipa are not involved.
Ed Newton-Rex quit Stability AI over its fair use position in its own US Copyright Office filing.
